description: Press Council Nepal objects to police intervention in media newsrooms  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Press Council Nepal (PCN) has expressed serious concern over reports that plainclothes police personnel entered the newsrooms of several media outlets, detained journalists and attempted to arrest them.

The Council strongly objected to the actions, which reportedly took place after office hours on Friday, ahead of two consecutive public holidays.

It said taking journalists into custody without providing clear grounds for arrest, presenting an arrest warrant, obtaining court authorization or disclosing the nature of the criminal complaint amounted to a serious threat to press freedom and journalists’ professional security.

The Council also recalled that it is legally mandated to investigate, monitor and address complaints arising from media content, disputes over published news and alleged violations of the journalistic code of conduct.

It urged the Government of Nepal, police authorities and other concerned parties to follow the Council’s established mechanisms and procedures to resolve such disputes rather than directly resorting to police intervention.

Furthermore, the Council demanded the immediate disclosure of the detained journalists’ status and the legal grounds for their arrest. It also called for their immediate release if they were being held without a valid legal basis.

At the same time, the Council urged media organizations and journalists to strictly adhere to the journalistic code of conduct and ensure that all published content is accurate, factual and evidence-based.

Researchers from Cornell University, WWF Nepal and local forest authorities in Nepal are testing lab-made versions of big-cat scent chemicals, which they call “BioBoundaries,” an attempt to create a chemical fence to keep big cats away from livestock.

Some experiment sites report that tigers and leopards approach the scent stations, investigate them and often turn back without crossing. KATHMANDU — In March 2025, a tiger followed a forest trail through Nepal’s Khata Corridor until it reached a small iron stake next to the path. Attached to it was a dispenser releasing a laboratory-made version of a chemical found in the scent markings big cats use to mark their territory and communicate with other cats.

A camera trap recorded the Bengal tiger ( Panthera tigris tigris) approaching the station. The curious cat investigated the smell and then stopped, one of multiple instances of tigers and leopards coming up to these scent stations and then turning back the way they came.

These encounters offer an early glimpse into an international experiment seeking to harness big cats’ territorial instinct in order to keep them away from livestock, farms and human settlements. But researchers caution that a tiger turning away from an experimental station is not yet solid evidence that the method can prevent livestock attacks.

“It’s a long way from proving that — and we don’t claim otherwise,” said Martin Gilbert, a wildlife veterinarian, epidemiologist and associate professor at Cornell University in the U.S. who helped bring the research to Nepal. “At this stage, we’re asking a more fundamental question: Can these compounds reliably alter a predator’s behavior?”

A woman with her goats in the buffer area in Bardiya. Image by Tulsi Rauniyar for Mongabay.

Across Nepal’s buffer-zone settlements, encounters with tigers, leopards and snow leopards have led communities to use electric fences, flashing lights and other deterrents to protect livestock and homes. Large carnivores, however, may learn that lights and sounds pose no threat, while fences are expensive to build and maintain. Livestock also risk vulnerability if farmers allow them to graze in forests or when they’re kept in weak sheds.

Researchers are now testing synthetic versions of chemicals that big cats use to mark territory and communicate with one another. Released from small dispensers, the compounds are intended to influence predator movements and create what the team calls “BioBoundaries” — invisible scent-based borders around vulnerable areas.

So far, there have been mixed results. “The animals approached and investigated the scent but did not cross the perceived boundary,” said Shashank Poudel, head of the wildlife program at WWF Nepal. “Other compounds produced the opposite response: Instead of turning away, the tigers became more interested and visited the site more frequently. That was not the intended outcome. Another compound appeared more promising as a deterrent for leopards.”

The research team installing scent dispensers on a tree. Image courtesy of WWF Nepal.

Tests in Botswana

The idea of using artificial territorial signals originated in Botswana in the mid-1990s, when wildlife biologist Tico McNutt proposed using long-lasting scent marks to discourage African wild dogs ( Lycaon pictus ) from leaving protected areas.

Chemical engineer Peter Apps later began developing scent-based deterrents after camera-trap footage in 2016 recorded a leopard making a U-turn upon encountering a component of leopard urine. Apps, now a senior researcher at the field research program Botswana Predator Conservation (BPC), used gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to identify chemicals in leopard urine. This laboratory technique separates, identifies and measures chemical compounds in a sample. He then tested commercially available versions of the chemicals on wild carnivores.

“We artificially create simplified equivalents of the chemical signals that predators use to mark their territories and communicate socially, and then use them to influence predators’ movements,” Apps told Mongabay.

In Botswana, Apps said, one compound known as 3M3MB substantially reduced leopard attacks on livestock. Gilbert said these findings persuaded him that the approach can be tested elsewhere, although he cautioned against assuming that it would work across different species and ecosystems.

“I wouldn’t say we were convinced they would work — that’s what the research is designed to find out,” Gilbert said. “What interested us was evidence from Botswana that a naturally occurring component of leopard scent could alter leopard behavior.”

An African wild dog in Botswana. Image by Derek Keats via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0).

Mixed signals from Nepal’s big cats

Cornell University, WWF Nepal, and forest authorities in Bardiya National Park and the Dolpa district in western Nepal launched a three-year trial supported by a dozen field personnel. Researchers began testing 10 compounds at treated and control stations in the Khata Corridor — a 13-kilometer (8-mile) stretch of land that links Bardia National Park with India’s Katarniaghat Wildlife Sanctuary — in October 2024. In the research, the treated group received the substance or intervention being tested, while the control group did not, allowing researchers to compare outcomes and assess its effects.

However, the experiment in Nepal was not a replication of Apps’ earlier leopard trials. Of the compounds tested in Nepal, only 3M3MB had previously been tested in Botswana, Apps said. Most of the substances had originally been identified in tiger scents. One compound that reduced leopard camera detections in Nepal subsequently produced a similar effect in Botswana.

The results were mixed. The compounds triggered similar levels of avoidance in tigers and leopards, measured by a decline in camera-trap videos, according to Apps. Three compounds produced this response in leopards and two in tigers. Apps said most of the substances tested had been identified in the tiger scent, so he was not surprised that tigers investigated the odors more closely than leopards did. Tigers sniffed intensely and displayed flehmen, a behavior used to investigate chemical signals, much as they would when examining natural scent marks. Some also turned back around after sniffing the test odors, suggesting they may have interpreted them as territorial scent marks, Apps said.

“The tiger responses provide evidence that scent signals can influence the behavior of another large felid, while the differences between leopards in Botswana and Nepal tell us that we shouldn’t assume responses will be universal,” Gilbert said.

A tiger in Bardiya National Park, 2021. Image by AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha.

Babu Ram Lamichhane, a wildlife researcher at the nonprofit Wild Care Nepal who is not involved in the trial, said territorial behavior does not necessarily prevent tigers from using the same space. Examining tiger census data, he had found up to seven tigers recorded at the same location, although they could use the area at different times.

“We will need to monitor their behavior closely to determine whether this method can be effective,” he said.

The team reduced the selection from 10 compounds to six for a second phase conducted between December 2025 and June 2026. But it was delayed due to Nepal’s recent national tiger census and demands on field personnel.

In the Khata Corridor, the team installed 30 stations, each consisting of an iron stake, a scent dispenser and a camera trap. The compounds are released at rates measured in millionths of a gram per hour. Local citizen scientists inspect the stations and help collect footage and field observations.

Lamichhane also raised questions about how the scents would perform under different weather conditions. They might be stronger in dry conditions, he said, while rain and moisture could affect how they disperse. “Effectiveness would also depend on where dispensers are placed, how closely they are spaced and the area they cover,” he told Mongabay.

In the Khata Corridor, the team installed 30 stations, each consisting of an iron stake, a scent dispenser and a camera trap. Image courtesy of WWF Nepal.

Researchers leave dispensers empty during control periods and install the equipment weeks before testing begins. These measures help distinguish responses to the chemical from curiosity or fear caused by an unfamiliar object appearing in a cat’s home territory. Researchers also need to see reactions repeated among different animals and detect a measurable change in movement of animals before inferring a behavioral effect.

Locals in Khata Corridor have tried early warning sirens, watchtowers and wire fencing to protect people, crops and livestock from wild animals, said Hari Gurung, chair of Khata Community Forest Coordination Committee (KCFCC), which represents 39 community forests. He said artificial scent could deter leopards, though he was not sure it would work against tigers. “If the results are positive, we could use it to protect livestock from predators,” he said. “It could become one of several measures to reduce human-wildlife conflict.”

The compounds researchers used triggered similar levels of avoidance in tigers and leopards, measured by a decline in camera-trap videos. Image courtesy of WWF Nepal.

From animal behavior to livestock protection

If the scents prove effective, dispensers could be installed around corrals, near the settlements and other high-risk areas. Researchers could also attach scent dispensers to individual animals allowing a moving herd to carry a protective scent as they graze.

Apps said collar-mounted dispensers have reduced predation in Botswana. But the approach has not been tested in Nepal, and researchers must determine which applications suit the country’s livestock practices, landscapes and carnivore species.

Gilbert said scent deterrents would not remove the need for stronger sheds, appropriate herding and other safeguards.

“BioBoundaries aren’t intended to replace good livestock husbandry,” he said. “What we aim to develop is an additional tool that will complement those approaches, particularly in situations where it isn’t practical to eliminate all of the underlying risk.”

A farming couple with their water buffalo near Chitwan National Park. Their previous buffalo was killed by a tiger. Image by Jonas Gratzer for Mongabay.

Another concern is whether discouraging a predator from approaching one household could redirect it toward another corral or grazing area. Gilbert said future trials would have to operate across a sufficiently large area to determine whether BioBoundaries reduce conflict rather than redistribute it.

Predators could also learn that the synthetic scent is not accompanied by a territorial rival and begin ignoring it. Apps said African trials have shown little habituation after months of exposure, including one flock reportedly protected from leopard attacks for three years. Those findings have not yet been replicated in Nepal.

Habituation may be less likely because the compounds exploit an evolved communication system rather than presenting predators with an arbitrary frightening stimulus, Apps and Gilbert said. Nevertheless, their effectiveness over prolonged exposure still requires testing.

Researchers said they hope to identify several compounds that could be rotated or combined. Apps said mixtures might produce stronger effects, while keeping additional scents in reserve could help if animals eventually get used to a scent, and begin ignoring it. Whether rotation would preserve their effectiveness remains untested.

“We want not just one but a couple of compounds to work,” WWF Nepal’s Poudel said. “Then we can use them in rotation.”

He said some scents also caused wild boar, spotted deer and sambar to flee, raising an untested possibility that they might help protect crops from herbivores.

Even if researchers identify an effective scent, they must determine how frequently dispensers need refilling, how much it will cost, and who would manufacture, approve and distribute them. Poudel said veterinary services might eventually distribute the compounds, but Gilbert said designing such a system would be premature before researchers demonstrate both repeatable avoidance and fewer livestock attacks.

Domesticated yaks in Nepal. Free-roaming yaks in high elevations face the risk of snow leopard attacks. Image by Jerome Bon via Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

Maintenance would be a crucial test of any community application, Lamichhane said. “Most of our measures to prevent wild animals from destroying crops or killing livestock have failed because of a lack of maintenance.” Another concern was whether the chemicals could be produced in Nepal, he added.

“Ultimately, the system will need to be inexpensive, simple to deploy and practical for livestock owners to maintain [it] themselves,” Gilbert said. “Otherwise, it won’t be a viable conflict-mitigation tool.”

Poudel said no single technology could solve human-wildlife conflict. Changes in wildlife distribution, farming practices, grazing, forest use and human movement can all alter where and why conflicts occur.

“We often see conflict as a one-dimensional problem,” he said. “It is a wicked problem. There is no single solution.”

“As long as humans and wildlife live together, conflicts are bound to occur,” Poudel said. “Our goal should be to reduce the harm.”

It is also a city shaped by people from every corner of Nepal," Dangol said, as per Variety.She added, "Over generations, communities from across the country have brought their traditions, languages, art, music and stories to Kathmandu. That coming together is what makes this city so vibrant and unique."Dangol also highlighted the significance of cinema and storytelling in the aftermath of Nepal's recent floods."Nepal has been through a profound tragedy with the floods, and in moments like these, stories become even more important," she said, adding, "They help us make sense of what we have experienced, connect with one another, heal and find the courage to move forward."

By TRN Online, Kathmandu, Oct 30: Three members of the French Military High Mountain Group (GMHM), based in Chamonix (France), have opened a new route on the North face of Peak 41 (6,654 m) .

The team included Sergeant Piontek, Corporal Fouillade and Corporal Paulin. They climbed for four days on technical terrain. The route is 1,400 meters long. The route has been named as "Bon Matin" ("Good Morning" in French) , according to a press release issued by the French Embassy in Nepal.

The climbers completed the ascent on 14 October 202 6 in alpine style by carrying their own equipment and supplies, using no fixed camps, and no supplemental oxygen.

Nepal and France share a long history in the mountains. On 3 June 1950, Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal reached the summit of Annapurna I. It was the first ascent of an 8,000 m peak in history. This new route continues that shared tradition.

title: San Diego nonprofit completes medical mission to flood-ravaged Nepal - 10News.com
description: San Diego nonprofit completes medical mission to flood-ravaged Nepal  10News.com
publisher.title: 10News.com
full_article:
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) - A medical mission led by a San Diego-area nonprofit has wrapped up its work in flood-ravaged Nepal, where volunteers faced washed-out roads, landslides and an unexpected emergency involving a bear attack victim.

Michael Sohmer, a retired clinical pharmacist and co-founder of the global health nonprofit Sweeping Change, traveled to Nepal as part of a 17-member medical mission following deadly flash floods that devastated parts of the country.

ABC 10News first spoke with Sohmer last month as he prepared for the trip. Having coordinated previous medical missions to Nepal, he expected significant needs in communities affected by the disaster.

After the ABC 10News story aired, donations poured into a GoFundMe campaign to help purchase supplies for the mission.

“What comes up for me is just gratitude,” Sohmer said.

Once Sohmer arrived in Kathmandu several weeks ago, however, the mission faced an immediate obstacle: The team's planned route had become impassable.

“The route we were going to take was washed out. There were landslides. It was raining. It continued to rain,” Sohmer said. “I was looking up at the heavens and hoping the rain would finally stop.

Conditions improved after several days, allowing the team to travel using alternate routes. Sohmer then rented a helicopter to transport the medical team and its supplies to Nepal's Rasuwa District, north of Kathmandu.

When they arrived, the team was confronted with another emergency.

A local resident had suffered a serious wound in a bear attack.

“At that point, I made the decision I was going to put him in the helicopter back to Kathmandu for care,” he said.

The team then established its clinic and treated nearly 400 people over the next four days.

“There were infections. Many had been cut off from medications,” said Sohmer.

The mountainous community had been cut off from access to medical care by the flooding, according to Sohmer. Many residents were also grieving relatives lost in the disaster.

“There was a lot of depression, a lot of psychological services I wish I would have been able to provide,” Sohmer said.

With the mission completed, Sohmer is planning to return to San Diego next week. He is already looking ahead to another trip to Nepal, with plans to raise money to return in April 2027 to provide medical and dental services.

title: Nepal, Indonesia sign MoU to strengthen mountain guiding standards - The Tourism Times
description: Nepal, Indonesia sign MoU to strengthen mountain guiding standards  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) and the Indonesian Mountaineering Federation (FMI) have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to strengthen cooperation in mountain guiding, climbing, mountaineering education and safety.

The agreement was signed in Kathmandu on Friday by NNMGA President Tul Singh Gurung and FMI President Major General (Retd) Buyung Lalana. Delegates from Indonesia and officials of the NNMGA attended the signing ceremony.

The partnership aims to improve professional mountain guiding standards, promote technical cooperation and develop training programmes in climbing and mountaineering. Both organisations plan to exchange knowledge, expertise and best practices to improve safety and develop skilled human resources for the mountain tourism sector.

The agreement is also expected to create opportunities for technical training, capacity building and the development of mountaineering education programmes suited to the needs of both countries.

The Indonesian delegation included FMI Deputy President Brigadier General Sandy Muchjitin Latef, General Secretary Dr M Iqbal El Mubarak, Deputy General Secretary Colonel Arief Rehman Haleim and other federation officials. Upendra Ghimire, honorary vice-consul of Indonesia in Nepal, was also present.

Representing the NNMGA were immediate past president Ang Norbu Sherpa, Vice-President Lakpa Sherpa, General Secretary Pimba Tenjing Lama, Treasurer Abiral Rai and members of its central executive board and technical committee, along with senior instructors.

The two organisations said they intended to build a long-term partnership to advance mountaineering education, improve safety standards and facilitate the exchange of technical expertise between Nepal and Indonesia.

NAYA PADAMPUR, Nepal — A spinning wheel whirs on a rooftop in Naya Padampur in south-central Nepal, sending ivory strands of yarn through Bin Maya Gurung’s practiced fingers. Smile lines crinkle at the corners of her eyes as she works. Her limbs move in synchrony with the wheel, both integral parts of the machine that ensures her family’s well-being.

She’s sitting at the top of a building that houses a wool spinning enterprise, which has blossomed in the years since she learned to spin wool in the early 2000s. It’s one of many women-led microenterprises that have sprouted across the country.

The past few decades have seen many women in rural Nepal venture into the business environment for the first time, as governmental regulations and societal norms started to shift. The benefits for women entrepreneurs are significant, with a 2022 study conducted in the Parbat district of Nepal showing that 96% of women involved in microenterprises felt confident in supporting their families with the money they earned.

The microenterprises are also important in another way: They provide an alternative source of income to rural families, lessening their reliance on forest products such as timber.

Successful women-led microenterprises — in Nepal and elsewhere — have provided a symbiosis between land and community, allowing conservation efforts to flourish while acting as a catalyst for local income generation and women’s empowerment.

The growth of these microenterprises in Nepal mirrors a growing global recognition of the benefits of women’s involvement in both forests and enterprise. Many women-led microenterprises harvest non-timber forest products with low impact or even a beneficial impact to forest systems. Others, like the spinning enterprise, lessen a household’s reliance on forest products altogether.

But for many Nepali women, social, financial and regulatory hurdles make it an uphill climb to get these businesses off the ground.

The sign outside the enterprise headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

From the ground up

When Gurung arrived in Naya Padampur, her income source became a risky endeavor.

Gurung, now 73, had been part of a settlement called Padampur, which was located within the boundaries of what is now Chitwan National Park, home to vulnerable and endangered species such as single-horned Asiatic rhinoceroses ( Rhinoceros unicornis ), Bengal tigers ( Panthera tigris tigris ) and gharials ( Gavialis gangeticus ). In the 1990s, the Nepali government ordered the relocation of Padampur residents to a place outside the park — the place that is now Naya (new) Padampur.

Gurung remembers her early days in Naya Padampur well. The area was freshly deforested for the settlement. There were very few resources for the residents, and no irrigation systems for farming. Rhinos came close to their houses and roamed across the area nearby.

Gurung’s main source of income for the family at that time was raksi, a traditional Nepali spirit. In order to make the liquor, she was forced to travel into the forest directly outside of the Naya Padampur settlement to fetch firewood, a process made vastly more dangerous because of the proximity of wild animals such as rhinos and tigers. Gurung faced the possibility of wildlife encounters and attacks on these daily trips.

Women in rural Nepal still face an elevated risk of wildlife attacks because their daily tasks, such as collecting water and firewood, often take them directly to the forest edge. A 2026 study found that while women made up less than half of the total tiger attacks in Nepal from 2010-24, the fatality rate of wildlife attacks on women exceeded 70%, whereas the fatality rate in men was under 50%.

Gurung took that risk every day to bring income home.

Bin Maya Gurung sits in the enterprise’s headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

At the time of the relocation, there was a general push toward community forestry and community-centric conservation. Nepal passed the Forest Act in 1993, which allowed community forest groups to take over the management of state-owned national forests in their areas. Today, community forest user groups manage around one-third of total forest cover in Nepal, giving agency back to local communities.

There were also many NGOs providing training and funding for the development of microenterprises in Nepal’s rural communities. Two examples were the U.N. Development Programme’s Micro Enterprise Development Programme and programs from the National Trust for Nature Conservation in Nepal (NTNC), which sought to increase community involvement in conservation and provide workshops for women focused on business literacy and marketable skills.

Around Chitwan, these businesses now focus on everything from elephant grass weaving and soap making to beekeeping and nature guiding. Many of the enterprises utilize non-timber forest products for income, according to a case study by the Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN). These businesses — which can produce eco-friendly products such as bamboo baskets, candles and nettle powder, or products such as coffee and bamboo — can actually benefit the larger ecosystem in many ways, CDKN wrote in their study, as well as stimulating the economy.

“Planting of bamboo, coffee, and broom grass on fallow land has supported soil conservation, while the establishment of a permanent tree nursery by a women’s cooperative has helped prevent soil erosion and landslides,” CDKN wrote.

Gurung saw a future free from her reality at the time. She knew of the NTNC and other NGO workshops, and she’d seen women engaged in wool spinning in other communities. She thought if she could get a workshop together, she could leave behind the dangers of wildlife encounters on her treks to the forest. So she gathered 25 women and contacted the NTNC.

That wool spinning workshop marked the start of Gurung’s business journey, one that has stretched over the past two decades. It’s given her freedom from the risky work she used to undertake and brought a powerful source of revenue to her family. It’s allowed her to finance her grandson’s university education and start three different bank accounts to save up money for her family’s future. And it’s greatly diminished her firewood collecting.

During a spinning workshop Gurung was teaching, she mentored Buddhimaya Ghale, who is now the head of the spinning business, which employs 600 women within the Naya Padampur area and another 300 across Nepal. The women involved in the project make anywhere from 8,000-40,000 Nepalese rupees ($52-$263) per month depending on the amount of time they can devote to the handicrafts. The business also offers trainings in wool spinning.

When women are involved in microenterprises, their social status changes, Ghale said. They are able to assert themselves as decision-makers in the household because they provide income for the family. As they slowly emerge as business leaders, they are able to assert their independence more freely.

Sanjay Chaudhary, co-founder of the Tharu Community Women’s Hand, an organization that provides handicraft and business skills workshops for women in the Indigenous Tharu community in the surrounding Chitwan area, said his wife and sister have both been able to establish themselves as entrepreneurs in the community. They actively voice their opinions in town and at meetings, and it’s led others in the community to perceive them differently.

“They’re more empowered, and they started challenging so many social norms, and it’s very good that they’ve started questioning so many conventional narratives,” Chaudhary said.

Buddhimaya Ghale sits behind her desk at the enterprise’s headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

An uphill climb

The stories of successful women entrepreneurs speak for themselves. But despite the economic and social benefits, many women remain on the outskirts.

Ghale said the journey into the workplace is not an easy one for women. In many cases, they first need to persuade their families to support their endeavors. Ghale had to strike out on her own to find work for the first time, since her husband did not approve.

After their struggles in the home, Chaudhary said women often face increased scrutiny due to Nepal’s traditionally masculine business environment. In the process of securing loans or other necessary steps to starting a business, he said women will often be asked where their husband is, or judged based on whether they have a good family.

Another hurdle is property rights, Chaudhary said. Only about 20% of women in rural Nepal own land, according to a 2026 study conducted by the Climate Policy Initiative, which makes providing collateral for the bank extremely difficult.

The government has tried multiple strategies to address this, according to Arjun Chapagain, who works as a sustainable forest management coordinator for the Federation of Community Forestry Users Nepal. Nepal’s new Constitution in 2015 granted equal rights to land ownership for men and women. But Chapagain said the reality has yet to catch up with the new policies.

“Even [in] that case, the people just keep only their name here, but again, the control is with the man,” Chapagain said.

The government has also created specific subsidized loans for women entrepreneurs, Chaudhary said. One example of this is a homeownership loan by Nabil Bank designed specifically for women.

But the same study from the Climate Policy Initiative suggests that these loans are still proving elusive for women. According to their report, 88% of the women surveyed in the study relied on personal savings to start their businesses, and only 56% had accessed formal finance.

“This broadly reflects the cumulative impact of cumbersome application processes, stringent evaluation criteria, lack of guarantors, limited advisory support, geographic constraints, and gender bias—particularly for smaller enterprises,” the authors wrote.

And in order to access business loans, microenterprises must be formally registered. A 2026 World Bank Group report evaluating the benefits of formalization found that for about 78% of informal microenterprises, the costs accrued for formal microenterprises would outweigh the benefits of formalization. The Kathmandu Post reported statistics from the Nepal Department of Industry showing that the rate of new registrations for microenterprises has plummeted nearly 75% in five years.

Without scale-specific interventions, the World Bank argues it will be difficult for these enterprises to reach their true growth potential — instead remaining a subsistence income to keep families afloat.

A spinning wheel sits on a table inside the enterprise’s headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

Enterprise and conservation

Yet Chaudhary said prioritizing these enterprises may be the key to getting reluctant communities on board with new environmental regulations. Living in Chitwan’s buffer zones, such as Chaudhary’s home in Sauhara, comes with heavy restrictions on fishing, hunting and collecting firewood. At the moment, he said his community has quite a bit of negative sentiment toward conservation due to those restrictions.

“If the park administrations could promote or motivate women for forest-based … enterprises, then that could be the biggest strength,” Chaudhary said. “That could help to make the mindset or narratives positive.”

In addition to the societal benefits, enterprises such the elephant grass handicrafts taught at the Tharu Community Women’s Hand use forest resources highly efficiently, Chaudhary said, with minimal impact on the landscape. Instead of chopping timber, the women simply harvest grasses for their handicrafts, and a small amount of grass can go a long way. Their organization also collaborates with local mahouts, or elephant handlers, Chaudbury said. The mahouts harvest elephant grasses for the microenterprise trainings on their regular forest patrols, so women do not need to make the risky journey into the forest.

After years of wool spinning, Gurung said she rarely visits the forest. Her livelihood no longer relies on forest products. She can feel her body start to age and slow down, but her work is something she can continue in her old age.

Gurung set the spinning wheel in motion. Now her legacy runs through each thread of the group’s handicrafts, and wheels across Nepal will spin long after she is gone.

Woven rugs created by the spinning enterprise lean against the wall at the business headquarters in Naya Padampur. Image courtesy of Nadia White.

title: Nepal to help Indonesia develop international-standard mountain guides - Everest Chronicle
description: Nepal to help Indonesia develop international-standard mountain guides  Everest Chronicle
publisher.title: Everest Chronicle
full_article:
The Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) and the Indonesian Mountaineering Federation (FMI) have signed an agreement to strengthen cooperation in mountain guiding, mountaineering education, technical training and safety.

The agreement, signed in Kathmandu on Friday by NNMGA President Tul Singh Gurung and FMI President Major General (Retd) Buyung Lalana, aims to promote professional mountain guiding standards and facilitate the exchange of technical expertise between the two organisations.

The partnership aims to improve professional mountain guiding standards, develop skilled human resources and promote international best practices in climbing and mountaineering safety.

“It is a matter of honour for us to enter into an agreement with FMI to assist them in training for international-standard mountaineering courses,” Gurung said.

Established in 2005, the NNMGA has been training professional mountain guides and represents Nepal at the International Federation of Mountain Guides Associations (IFMGA), also known as UIAGM.

Nepal is among only three Asian countries represented in the international federation, alongside Japan and Kyrgyzstan.

IFMGA-certified Nepali guides have conducted mountaineering courses in several Asian countries, both independently and through institutional projects.

The agreement marks a major international collaborative initiative for the NNMGA, which said it hoped to establish a long-term partnership with Indonesia through technical training, capacity building and mountaineering education programmes tailored to the needs of both countries.

The Indonesian delegation included FMI Deputy President Brigadier General Sandy Muchjitin Latef, General Secretary Dr M Iqbal El Mubarak and Deputy General Secretary Colonel Arief Rehman Haleim. Upendra Ghimire, Indonesia's honorary vice-consul in Nepal, also attended the ceremony.

The NNMGA delegation included immediate past president Ang Norbu Sherpa, Vice-President Lakpa Sherpa, General Secretary Pimba Tenjing Lama, Treasurer Abiral Rai and members of its executive board, technical committee and senior instructors.

In a joint statement, the organisations said they intended to build a long-term partnership to advance mountaineering education, improve safety standards and facilitate the exchange of technical expertise.

The cooperation could also open opportunities for Nepali mountain guides to contribute to mountaineering development in Indonesia, home to Carstensz Pyramid, a 4,884-metre peak in Papua and the highest mountain in Oceania.

Carstensz Pyramid is one of the Seven Summits, the highest mountains on each of the world's seven continents, and attracts climbers seeking to complete the mountaineering challenge. Nepali guides also lead expeditions to the peak.

title: Nepal’s U.N. Envoy Meets Guterres, Thanks U.N. for Flood Aid and Calls for Stronger Climate Action - nepyork
description: Nepal’s U.N. Envoy Meets Guterres, Thanks U.N. for Flood Aid and Calls for Stronger Climate Action  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
NEW YORK — Nepal’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Lok Bahadur Thapa, met Wednesday with U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, praising his leadership and commitment to multilateralism and thanking the United Nations for its assistance following devastating floods in Nepal.

During the meeting, Thapa commended Guterres’ principled leadership, commitment to multilateralism and efforts to promote international solidarity and ensure no one is left behind, according to a statement from the Nepali envoy.

Thapa reaffirmed Nepal’s commitment to the U.N. Charter, multilateral cooperation and collective action to address global challenges. He also expressed appreciation for assistance from the U.N. system following recent climate-related disasters in Nepal.

Guterres expressed condolences for the loss of lives and property caused by the disasters and acknowledged Nepal’s active role in advancing multilateral cooperation, according to the statement.

The secretary-general recognized Nepal’s contributions to several key international initiatives, including its presidency of the U.N. Economic and Social Council, chairmanship of the group of least developed countries, facilitation of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development and chairmanship of the U.N. General Assembly’s First Committee.

He also praised Nepal’s advocacy for climate action and its longstanding contributions to international peace and security as one of the leading contributors of troops and police personnel to U.N. peacekeeping missions.

Recalling his visit to the base camp of Mount Everest three years ago, Guterres highlighted the devastating effects of climate change in the Himalayas and stressed the need for urgent and ambitious global climate action, the statement said.

Both sides emphasized the importance of strengthening early warning systems, improving resilience to climate-related disasters and promoting greater international solidarity and cooperation to advance global climate goals.

title: Nepal comes up with four proposals for dealing with mountain crises, 53 nations back them - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal comes up with four proposals for dealing with mountain crises, 53 nations back them  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 30: Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, has said that the crises caused by climate change in the Himalayan region are not confined within the geographical boundaries of just one country.

At a high-level regional dialogue organized on Thursday in Bangkok by the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and the Government of Nepal under the title 'From Everest to the Sea,' he said that global cooperation is necessary for mountain conservation.

Minister Shrestha's secretariat has stated that representatives from 53 countries have supported the four proposals that Nepal presented to the international community to reduce the impacts of climate change and manage cross-border disaster risks.

Nepal has emphasized the need to develop a multi-hazard early warning system based on satellites, artificial intelligence (AI), and modern technology, through collaboration between international space agencies, scientific institutions, and the government, to monitor risky mountain slopes and glaciers.

Minister Shrestha also mentioned that Prime Minister Balendra Shah proposed the 'Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism' for coordinating information exchange, glacier monitoring, and early warning systems in the Himalayan region.

Minister Shrestha emphasized that immediate financial assistance should be made available for disaster risk reduction, preparedness, and recovery, and that it should be accessible and grant-based.

He said that in high Himalayan areas, monitoring and early warning should be supported through grants, not loans, and investments in riverside hydropower projects to border towns should be managed by considering the risks from the source to the sea.((RSS)
